title: 25% of Nepali Removal Orders Over 28 Years Issued Under Trump in 18 Months; Relief-Grant Rate Falls to 7.6% - nepyork
description: 25% of Nepali Removal Orders Over 28 Years Issued Under Trump in 18 Months; Relief-Grant Rate Falls to 7.6%  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
In just 18 months, U.S. immigration courts issued 1,162 removal orders to Nepali nationals between January 2025 and June 2026—accounting for 25% of all removal orders recorded for the group over the past 28 years, according to Executive Office for Immigration Review records compiled by TRAC.

When combined with Donald Trump’s first presidential term, courts have issued a total of 2,006 removal orders to Nepali nationals across both terms, representing 43.24% of the 4,639 total removal orders recorded in the dataset since 1998. In fiscal year 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal year 2026, removal orders remained the dominant outcome in the Nepal docket, far outpacing grants of relief and case closures.

Relief Granted at 7.6%

For fiscal year 2025, the data show 1,837 total case hearings involving Nepalis. Of those, judges issued 569 removal orders and granted relief in 378 cases—which represents 20.58% of total hearings. Additionally, 249 cases were terminated, and 223 were recorded as “no Notice to Appear (NTA) filed.”

Other outcomes included 185 credible-fear cases in which fear was not found, 94 credible-fear cases in which fear was found, 87 voluntary departures, and 23 other closures. Smaller categories included 13 “credible-fear other” cases, 11 “withholding-only other” cases, two prosecutorial-discretion outcomes, two “asylum-only other” cases, and one “withholding-only” case not granted.

Removal orders were the single largest outcome in fiscal year 2025, followed by grants of relief and terminations. Grants accounted for just over one in five total outcomes (20.58%), or 39.92% of direct merits decisions.

For the first nine months of fiscal year 2026, the Nepal docket recorded 941 total case hearings through the reporting period. Judges issued 634 removal orders, while 88 cases were terminated, 73 ended in voluntary departure, and 72 resulted in grants of relief, representing 7.65% of total hearings. Other outcomes included 30 credible-fear cases in which fear was not found, 29 “no NTA filed” cases, six other closures, five credible-fear cases in which fear was found, three “credible-fear other” cases, and one asylum-only case in which relief was not granted.

The fiscal year 2026 figures show an even more removal-heavy outcome mix than fiscal year 2025. Removal orders accounted for the clear majority of resolved cases, while grants of relief fell to a much smaller share of the docket—accounting for just 7.65% of total outcomes and 10.20% of direct merits decisions.

Removal orders for Nepali nationals in U.S. immigration courts rose sharply in fiscal years 2025 and 2026, according to Executive Office for Immigration Review records compiled by TRAC.

The pace of removal orders for Nepali nationals has climbed dramatically in the most recent period. Judges issued 1,162 removal orders between January 2025 and June 2026, representing more than a quarter of the total recorded over 28 years and far exceeding the totals registered under the Biden administration and Trump’s first term.

In calendar year 2025 alone, judges issued 783 removal orders for Nepali nationals, with the monthly total rising from 26 in January to a high of 112 in October. In the first six months of calendar year 2026, immigration judges issued another 379 removal orders, keeping the monthly pace at an average of nearly 63 orders.

Judges issued 644 removal orders for Nepali nationals during the Biden administration, from January 2021 through December 2024, and 864 during Trump’s first term, from January 2017 through December 2020. The 2025 total alone exceeded the four-year Biden total.

Historical Relief Grant and Removal Trends

At the same time, relief grant totals for Nepali nationals have been volatile over the long term and notably lower in the most recent year. Courts recorded 720 grants of relief in 2023—the highest annual total on record—followed by 607 in 2024, before a sharp drop to 378 in 2025 and 72 in 2026. While courts were issuing more removal orders in 2025 and 2026, they were granting relief at a far lower rate than during the 2023 peak.

The grant-of-relief pattern has fluctuated widely over time. Totals were 14 in 1998, 35 in 2001, 41 in 2002, 65 in 2003, 103 in 2004, and 96 in 2005 before rising to 180 in 2006 and 189 in 2009. Relief grants later climbed to 251 in 2010, 343 in 2011, 436 in 2012, and 445 in 2013, holding in the 300s through much of the mid-2010s before peaking in 2023.

Relief grants for Nepali nationals rose and fell over time, reaching 720 in 2023 before dropping to 378 in 2025 and 72 in 2026, according to TRAC-compiled EOIR records.

A fiscal-year view of the removal-order data reveals a similar upward trend, with 569 removal orders in fiscal year 2025 and 634 in fiscal year 2026, both well above earlier peaks. Those totals outpaced previous high-water marks, such as 349 in fiscal year 2019, 237 in fiscal year 2011, 218 in fiscal year 2018, and 204 in fiscal year 2023.

Removal orders for Nepali nationals were relatively modest in the late 1990s and early 2000s before gradually rising. The dataset includes 28 orders in 1998, 42 in 1999, 50 in 2000, 31 in 2001, 34 in 2002, 49 in 2003, and 66 in 2004. Orders then climbed to 94 in 2005, 95 in 2006, 88 in 2007, and 100 in 2008.

The numbers increased further in the 2010s, with 122 in 2009, 129 in 2010, 237 in 2011, 180 in 2012, 183 in 2013, 187 in 2014, 127 in 2015, 107 in 2016, 139 in 2017, 218 in 2018, and 349 in 2019. The total dipped to 170 in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic before rising again to 48 in 2021, 163 in 2022, 204 in 2023, and 196 in 2024, leading up to the sharp jump in 2025 and 2026.

The 783 orders in 2025 alone were more than four times the total from 2024 and nearly double the combined totals from 2021 and 2022.

(Editor’s note: This report uses two TRAC compiled Executive Office for Immigration Review data sets, one organized by fiscal year and one by calendar year, to more accurately reflect the Trump and Biden administrations.)

डोनाल्ड ट्रंप केरऽ पहलऽ राष्ट्रपति पद के साथ मिलाय क॑ कोर्ट न॑ दोनों कार्यकाल म॑ नेपाली नागरिकऽ क॑ कुल २,००६ हटाबै के आदेश जारी करलकै, जे १९९८ स॑ डाटासेट म॑ दर्ज ४,६३९ हटाबै के आदेशऽ म॑ स॑ ४३.२४% के प्रतिनिधित्व करै छै ।वित्तीय वर्ष २०२५ आरू वित्तीय वर्ष २०२६ केरऽ पहलऽ नौ महीना म॑ हटाबै के आदेश प्रमुख रहलऽ छै नेपाल डॉकेट मे परिणाम, राहत आ केस बंद करय के अनुदान सं बहुत आगू बढ़ि गेल.

7.6% पर राहत देल गेल

वित्तीय वर्ष 2025 के लेल आंकड़ा मे नेपाली सं जुड़ल कुल 1,837 मामला के सुनवाई भेल अछि. ओहि मे स न्यायाधीश 569 हटाबय क आदेश जारी केलथि आ 378 मामला मे राहत देलथि-जे कुल सुनवाई क 20.58% क प्रतिनिधित्व करैत अछि। एकरऽ अतिरिक्त, २४९ मामला समाप्त करलऽ गेलै, आरू २२३ मामला क॑ “कोनो नोटिस टू अपियर (एनटीए) दायर नै” के रूप म॑ दर्ज करलऽ गेलै ।

अन्य परिणामऽ म॑ १८५ विश्वसनीय-भय के मामला शामिल छेलै, जेकरा म॑ डर नै मिललै, ९४ विश्वसनीय-भय के मामला जेकरा म॑ डर मिललै, ८७ स्वैच्छिक प्रस्थान, आरू २३ अन्य बंदी । छोट श्रेणी मे 13 “विश्वसनीय-डर अन्य” मामला, 11 “केवल रोकय वाला अन्य” मामला, दू अभियोजक-विवेक परिणाम, दू “केवल शरण-अन्य” मामला, आ एकटा “केवल रोकय वाला” मामला शामिल नहि छल जे मंजूर नहि कएल गेल छल.

नेपयॉर्क कें मुफ्त मे सब्सक्राइब करू आब, अहां यू.एस.वीजा, ग्रीन कार्ड, आ सब आप्रवासन समाचारक कें कोनों अपडेट कें संग-संग आवास, कर, स्वास्थ्य देखभाल, आ बहुत किछु पर आवश्यक जानकारी आ संसाधनक कें सेहो छूटि नहिं जायब. एकरा सब के सीधा अपन इनबॉक्स में पहुंचा दियौ। ईमेल पता एतय दर्ज करू... सब्सक्राइब करय लेल एतय क्लिक करू

वित्तीय वर्ष 2025 म॑ हटाबै के आदेश एकलौता सबस॑ बड़ऽ परिणाम छेलै, जेकरा बाद राहत आरू समाप्ति के अनुदान मिललै । अनुदान कुल परिणामक मे सं पांच मे सं किछु बेसि (20.58%) यानी प्रत्यक्ष मेरिट निर्णयक कें 39.92% छल.

वित्तीय वर्ष 2026 क पहिल नौ मास लेल नेपाल डॉकेट मे रिपोर्टिंग अवधि क माध्यम स कुल 941 मामला क सुनवाई दर्ज कैल गेल। जज सब 634 हटाबय के आदेश जारी केलनि, जखन कि 88 मामला समाप्त भ गेल, 73 स्वैच्छिक प्रस्थान मे समाप्त भेल, आ 72 के परिणामस्वरूप राहत के अनुदान भेटल, जे कुल सुनवाई के 7.65% के प्रतिनिधित्व करैत अछि. अन्य परिणामऽ म॑ ३० विश्वसनीय-भय के मामला शामिल छेलै जेकरा म॑ डर नै मिललै, २९ “कोय एनटीए दायर नै करलऽ गेलऽ” केस, छह अन्य बंदी, ५ विश्वसनीय-डर केस जेकरा म॑ डर मिललै, तीन “विश्वसनीय-डर केस अन्य” मामला, आरू एक शरण-मात्र मामला जेकरा म॑ राहत नै देलऽ गेलऽ छेलै ।

वित्तीय वर्ष 2026 कें आंकड़ा वित्तीय वर्ष 2025 कें अपेक्षा आओर बेसि हटावय-भारी परिणाम मिश्रण कें दर्शा रहल छै.हटाबै कें आदेशक कें हिस्सा हल कैल गेल मामलाक कें स्पष्ट बहुमत छल, जखन कि राहत कें अनुदान डॉकेट कें बहुत कम हिस्सा मे गिर गेलय-कुल परिणामक कें मात्र 7.65% आ प्रत्यक्ष मेरिट निर्णयक कें 10.20% हिस्सा.

ट्रैक द्वारा संकलित आप्रवासन समीक्षा के कार्यकारी कार्यालय के रिकॉर्ड के अनुसार अमेरिकी आप्रवासन न्यायालय में नेपाली नागरिक के हटाबय के आदेश में वित्तीय वर्ष 2025 आ 2026 में भारी बढ़ोतरी भेल अछि।

नेपाली नागरिक के हटाबै के आदेश के गति सबसें ताजा अवधि में भारी बढ़ोत्तरी होय गेलऽ छै । जज न॑ जनवरी २०२५ आरू जून २०२६ के बीच १,१६२ हटाबै के आदेश जारी करलकै, जे २८ साल म॑ दर्ज कुल के एक चौथाई स॑ भी अधिक के प्रतिनिधित्व करै छै आरू बाइडेन प्रशासन आरू ट्रंप केरऽ पहलऽ कार्यकाल के तहत दर्ज कुल आदेश स॑ बहुत अधिक छै ।

मात्र कैलेण्डर वर्ष २०२५ मे न्यायाधीशसब नेपाली नागरिकके ७८३ हटबाक आदेश जारी केने छल, जाहिमे मासिक कुल संख्या जनवरीमे २६ सँ बढि अक्तूबरमे ११२ रहल अछि । कैलेंडर वर्ष 2026 केरऽ पहलऽ छह महीना म॑ आप्रवासन न्यायाधीश न॑ आरू 379 हटाबै के आदेश जारी करलकै, जेकरा स॑ औसतन लगभग 63 आदेश के मासिक गति बनलऽ रहलै ।

न्यायाधीश न॑ बाइडेन प्रशासन के दौरान, जनवरी २०२१ स॑ दिसंबर २०२४ तलक, नेपाली नागरिकऽ लेली ६४४ आरू ट्रंप केरऽ पहिलऽ कार्यकाल के दौरान, जनवरी २०१७ स॑ दिसंबर २०२० तलक ८६४ हटाबै के आदेश जारी करलकै ।अकेले २०२५ केरऽ कुल बाइडेन केरऽ चार साल केरऽ कुल आदेश स॑ अधिक छेलै ।

ऐतिहासिक राहत अनुदान एवं हटाने के प्रवृत्ति

एकरऽ साथ ही नेपाली नागरिकऽ लेली राहत अनुदान केरऽ कुल संख्या दीर्घकाल म॑ अस्थिर रहलऽ छै आरू सबसें हाल केरऽ साल म॑ उल्लेखनीय रूप स॑ कम छै । कोर्ट न॑ 2023 म॑ 720 राहत केरऽ अनुदान दर्ज करलकै- जे रिकॉर्ड म॑ सबस॑ अधिक वार्षिक कुल छै-जेकरा बाद 2024 म॑ 607 मिललै, जेकरा बाद 2025 म॑ 378 आरू 2026 म॑ 72 होय क॑ भारी गिरावट दर्ज करलऽ गेलै ।जहाँ कोर्ट न॑ 2025 आरू 2026 म॑ अधिक हटाबै के आदेश जारी करी रहलऽ छेलै, लेकिन ई दौरान के तुलना म॑ कहीं कम दर स॑ राहत द॑ रहलऽ छेलै २०२३ के शिखर।

समय के साथ राहत के अनुदान के पैटर्न म॑ काफी उतार-चढ़ाव रहलऽ छै । कुल संख्या 1998 मे 14, 2001 मे 35, 2002 मे 41, 2003 मे 65, 2004 मे 103, आ 2005 मे 96 छल, जखन कि 2006 मे 180 आ 2009 मे 189 भ गेल। बाद म॑ राहत अनुदान २०१० म॑ २५१, २०११ म॑ ३४३, २०१२ म॑ ४३६, आरू २०१३ म॑ ४४५ होय गेलै, जे २०२३ म॑ चरम पर पहुँचै स॑ पहल॑ २०१० केरऽ मध्य के अधिकांश समय तलक ३०० के दशक म॑ टिकलऽ रहलै ।

ट्रैक संकलित ईओआईआर रिकॉर्ड के अनुसार नेपाली नागरिक के राहत अनुदान समय के संग बढ़ल आ घटैत गेल, जे 2023 मे 720 पहुंच गेल, फेर 2025 मे 378 आ 2026 मे 72 भ गेल।

रिमूवल-ऑर्डर केरऽ आंकड़ा केरऽ वित्तीय वर्ष केरऽ दृष्टिकोण स॑ भी ऐसनऽ ही उछाल के रुझान सामने ऐलऽ छै, जेकरा म॑ वित्तीय वर्ष २०२५ म॑ ५६९ आरू वित्तीय वर्ष २०२६ म॑ ६३४ हटाबै के आदेश आबी गेलऽ छै, जे दोनों पहिने के चोटी स॑ काफी ऊपर छै । ओ कुल आंकड़ा पिछला उच्च जल निशान स आगू बढ़ल अछि, जेना वित्तीय वर्ष 2019 मे 349, वित्तीय वर्ष 2011 मे 237, वित्तीय वर्ष 2018 मे 218, आ वित्तीय वर्ष 2023 मे 204।

नेपाली नागरिक के हटाबै के आदेश धीरे-धीरे बढ़ै स॑ पहल॑ १९९० के दशक के अंत आरू २००० के दशक के शुरुआत म॑ अपेक्षाकृत मामूली छेलै । डाटासेट म॑ १९९८ म॑ २८, १९९९ म॑ ४२, २००० म॑ ५०, २००१ म॑ ३१, २००२ म॑ ३४, २००३ म॑ ४९, आरू २००४ म॑ ६६ ऑर्डर शामिल छै ।तखन॑ ऑर्डर २००५ म॑ ९४, २००६ म॑ ९५, २००७ म॑ ८८, आरू... 2008 मे 100।

2010 के दशक में ई संख्या आरू बढ़ी गेलै, 2009 में 122, 2010 में 129, 2011 में 237, 2012 में 180, 2013 में 183, 2014 में 187, 2015 में 127, 2016 में 107, 2017 में 139, 2018 मे 218, आ 2019 मे 349. कोविड-19 महामारी के दौरान 2020 मे 170 भ गेल 2026 के।

असगर 2025 मे 783 ऑर्डर 2024 क कुल स चारि गुना स बेसी अछि आ 2021 आ 2022 क कुल मिला कए लगभग दुगुना अछि।

(संपादक केरऽ नोट: ई रिपोर्ट म॑ ट्रंप आरू बाइडेन प्रशासन क॑ अधिक सटीक रूप स॑ दर्शाबै लेली दू ट्रैक द्वारा संकलित एक्जीक्यूटिव ऑफिस फॉर इमिग्रेशन रिव्यू डाटा सेट के उपयोग करलऽ गेलऽ छै, जेकरा म॑ एगो वित्तीय वर्ष के अनुसार आरू एक कैलेंडर वर्ष के अनुसार आयोजित करलऽ गेलऽ छै ।)

title: Nepal’s national ID outage disrupts passports, banking and government services - Biometric Update
description: Nepal’s national ID outage disrupts passports, banking and government services  Biometric Update
publisher.title: Biometric Update
full_article:
Nepal’s national identity infrastructure has seen extensive technical failures, leaving thousands unable to access services that are verified through the National Identity Management Information System (NIDMIS).

Since early July, 13 government agencies including the Department of Passports, banks, tax offices and immigration have suffered authentication problems via National Identity Numbers (NINs). Official departments have been forced to manually accept confirmation pages as a temporary workaround, reports The Kathmandu Post.

The Department of National ID and Civil Registration said new applicants were receiving NINs but their records were not being approved by the system, leading to widespread complaints. The department’s director general Krishna Poudel said IT teams, supported by French vendor IN Groupe, had been working for a week to restore functionality.

IN Groupe supplied both NIDMIS and Nepal’s Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS), and has now deployed specialists to Kathmandu, with officials expecting full restoration next week. Only two weeks ago, it was revealed that Nepali authorities had chosen IN Groupe for a new ABIS with the system upgraded for a capacity of 10 million biometric records.

The agreement seemed to have been struck with some urgency, as The Kathmandu Post reported the direct procurement bypassed normal tender procedures, allowed by the Public Procurement Act, and the license of the ABIS was said to have been nearing expiry with capacity left for only a few thousand data entries.

The outage leaves further questions as the government on May 8 cancelled a global tender for long‑term operation and maintenance of NIDMIS, choosing to manage the system in‑house instead. The government cited a push for digital sovereignty, even as it was reported technical evaluation was not completed before the tender was cancelled.

Reliance on national ID magnifies impact

Nepal has collected biometric data from around 20 million people, but only 7.8 million national identity cards have been printed, leaving millions waiting. Officials warn that delays are worsening as the card becomes mandatory for passports, banking, social security, driving licences, property transactions and university entrance exams.

The national identity card is now mandatory to conduct transactions using Nepal’s national digital payment system. The country’s central bank issued an amendment to this effect, with the aim of strengthening eKYC for all financial operations.

Nepal officials have formally lodged a proposal with Indian authorities requesting that its NID card be recognized as an official travel document, giving it the same status as passports. Nepal’s immigration director Ram Chandra Tiwari said the eventual aim was to replace citizenship certificates, which can also be used as travel documents for India, with the NIN entirely.

But this could all be stymied if the back-end infrastructure is not in place. Agencies linked to NIDMIS say they have repeatedly raised concerns about the slow response. Some have reported severe service backlogs, particularly at the Department of Passports, which has seen a surge in applicants following new migration labor openings in South Korea.

Banks have also been unable to update KYC records because national identity numbers cannot be verified. For now, the affected agencies have been instructed to continue providing services using enrollment confirmation pages until authentication is restored.

The disruption has drawn fresh concerns about Nepal’s ability to manage one of its largest digital infrastructure projects without external support. Earlier this year, the World Bank approved US$50 million to finance the build of digital public infrastructure with the funding going towards digital platforms and a new national identity system.

Nepal’s government has since argued that domestic control will strengthen data sovereignty, but officials inside the department claim they lack the expertise to recover from major failures.

title: Poets promote communal harmony - The Rising Nepal
description: Poets promote communal harmony  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Aug. 4: A literary gathering focused on religious harmony and humanism was jointly organised by the Bartaman Kabita Samuha and Nepali Folk Musical Instrument Museum in the capital on Sunday evening.

Held at the tranquil premises of the Nepali Folk Musical Instrument Museum at Teku, the event brought together a diverse group of poets, writers, and singers who utilised the power of creative expression to advocate for peace, unity, and mutual understanding.

The poetry recitation session featured a wide range of literary voices, each addressing the central themes of peace and humanism through distinct perspectives. Deepak Chaulagain opened the readings with 'Manisko Khoji', which depicted communal hatred as a destructive wildfire fanned by vested interests and highlighted the common person as the primary victim. Following him, Chachu Dungana recited 'Nara' (Slogan), drawing on his integrated upbringing to emphasise that sacred texts across faiths direct humanity towards honest duty rather than divisive political slogans.

Bina Nemkul presented 'Kalpanako Basti', using the non-discriminatory nature of air and earth to envision a society free from caste and creed. Prajwal Adhikari's 'Khelauna' offered a metaphorical critique of adult societal divides.

Further examining the fragile nature of life, Harihar Timilsina presented 'Malai Thaha Bhayeko Kura (The Things I Know), reminding the audience of the irreplaceable value of life and the equal right of all beings to coexist. Ishwara Shiwa’s 'Iswar-ko Hisab' argued that holy scriptures do not advocate violence, emphasising that true faith is measured by love and compassion rather than physical monuments. Highlighting selfless empathy, Avaya Shrestha's narrative poem 'Bhikshuni Ra Rogi Yuvak' (The Nun and the Sick Young Man) portrayed a protagonist assisting an ill youth across a river despite societal judgment, symbolising unconditional compassion.

Ram Gopal Ashutosh delivered 'Aagolai Aago Hun Kasaiko Jarurat Pardaina' (Fire Doesn't Need Anyone to Be Fire), warning leaders and citizens against spreading hatred. Pramod Snehi's 'Dharma Ra Yuddha' reflected on a society currently clouded by mistrust, expressing a yearning for hope.

Tirtharaj Bhatta recited 'Ke Hami Puna Buddha Banna Sakchhau ', questioning artificial divisions and urging a return to non-violence. Radhika Kalpit presented 'Marga Anek, Gantabya Ek', illustrating that while rituals across different faiths differ, they all share a singular destination of human service and peace. Rajani Mila’s 'Kaha Chha Iswar? Jagau Aafubhitra' criticised external searches for divinity, calling on individuals to cultivate internal tolerance and active compassion. Singer and composer Shishir Yogi then provided a musical interlude, performing Laxmi Prasad Devkota's socially conscious piece 'Damai Dai' and the acoustic song 'Lahar ko Boli' to reinforce the gathering's humanistic focus.

Chandra Bahadur Lama’s 'Sahisnutako Shaswat Niyam' (The Eternal Rule of Tolerance), which urged the audience to look beyond sectarian spaces to find shared empathy in the pure faith of daily life. The session host, poet Rami Priya, presented 'Manis Ra Dharma', illustrating nature's inherent equality and suggesting that sages historically treated natural elements as their mentors to connect humanity.

Bishwa Sigdel discussed the social responsibility of a writer, stating that history eventually questions what poets were doing during times of national crisis and whether they failed to address the challenges of their era. He concluded the poetry segment with 'Ma Je Bannuparne Thiyo', discussing a writer's historical responsibility and narrating a protagonist's realisation that adopting multiple religious labels is meaningless if one fails to remain a basic human being.

On behalf of the museum, Ram Prasad Kandel presented historical examples of interfaith cooperation, sharing a memory of spiritual leaders resolving a communal land dispute in Gorakhpur, India.

title: Resilient Highways - The Rising Nepal
description: Resilient Highways  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Persistent rainfall, landslides and flooding have disrupted vehicular movement on several major highways and road sections across the country. Each year, floods and landslides during the monsoon disrupt major highways of the country and before the roads are reconstructed, another monsoon takes a heavy toll on them. BP Highway, devastated by the 2024 flood and landslide, has not yet been repaired and reconstructed to date. Once again, the disrupted vehicular movement in major highways has highlighted fragile road infrastructure and inadequate disaster preparedness.





As per the news published in this daily, all types of vehicles have been prohibited from travelling along the Khurkot Nepalthok–Katunjebeshi section of the BP Highway from 6:00 pm to 4:00 am on Monday. Likewise, traffic has been suspended on the Kanti Lokpath between 5:00 pm and 5:00 am. In Ilam Municipality-9, the Mechi Highway has been completely closed after continuous rainfall turned the road muddy and unsafe for vehicles. The Araniko Highway has also been fully blocked following landslides at Zero Kilo and Kodari in Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality, Sindhupalchok.





Likewise, most of the highways in Nepal, including the East-West Highway, Madan Bhandari Highway, and Siddhicharan Lok Marga, have faced partial or major obstruction in the past few weeks. Travelling within the country has become extremely dangerous during the monsoon. The landslide in the Nagayanghat-Mugling road section is a regular occurrence. The vulnerable condition of the main route for the entrance has been an eyesore to the authorities.





Nepal's economy relies heavily on transportation or movement of agricultural goods. So when the major highways get disrupted, it has far-reaching economic consequences. When the supply chain breaks, it creates a shortage of essential goods, especially in Kathmandu and other major cities and a shortage of raw materials for businesses. Blockage of major highways during monsoon has been adversely affecting tourism, one of Nepal's key economic sectors. It has been working as a major deterrent for both domestic and international tourists. It has also tarnished Nepal's reputation as a safe travel destination for international tourists.





Although the Department of Roads and security forces work relentlessly to clear roads as soon as they get blocked, this emergency response alone is not a sustainable solution. Neither is it enough. The government should seek a long-term solution by building climate-resilient road infrastructure. Proper geological assessment, construction of a proper drainage system, and slope stabilization measures are a must. Haphazard blasting during road construction has made our mountains fragile, which aggravates landslides during the monsoon.





Today, we have strengthened early warning systems and improved weather forecasting. Likewise, people can get real-time information regarding road conditions. It has allowed authorities to mobilise resources before a disaster escalates.





The 2024 incident at Jhaplekhola has prompted people to take weather forecasts seriously before travelling during the peak monsoon period. For the past few years, we have been experiencing heavy rainfall over a short period of time. This leads to floods and landslides, which cause major damage to road infrastructure. Thus, the country should invest in resilient infrastructure, meeting international standards. Strengthening disaster preparedness is also a must to ensure undisrupted connectivity.

title: Players and legends urge action as Nepal risk first-ever absence from SAFF Championship - The Kathmandu Post
description: Players and legends urge action as Nepal risk first-ever absence from SAFF Championship  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
There are two countries that have participated in all 14 editions of the SAFF Men’s Championship to date—India and Nepal. That, however, might change this year. As Bangladesh are preparing to host the championship’s 15th edition in November, Nepal could miss playing at the biggest South Asian footballing event for the first time in history.

Nepal’s participation in South Asia’s premier international football tournament hinges on a critical condition: FIFA must lift the current suspension on the All Nepal Football Association before the stipulated SAFF deadline on September 30.

If that doesn’t happen, the beleaguered Nepali football would face another blow. Nepal have already missed out on five major football events this year.

Amid this, stakeholders have started pressuring the government—through social media—to help lift the FIFA suspension at the earliest.

“Honourable Prime Minister, today, the future of thousands of Nepali football players stands in jeopardy,” Hari Khadka, ANFA’s technical director, wrote on his Facebook on Sunday afternoon. “If a timely solution is not found, Nepal faces the grim reality of missing out on the upcoming SAFF Football Championship as well.”

Khadka, who is Nepal’s all-time joint highest goal scorer, added, “To safeguard years of hard work, dreams, and national pride of our athletes, I respectfully request you to consult with the concerned stakeholders, take the necessary initiatives, and foster an environment where Nepali players can step onto the pitch once again.”

The South Asian Football Federation has shown extreme flexibility towards Nepal. “In the event that Nepal’s FIFA suspension is lifted by September 30, Nepal will be included in the group of the hosts Bangladesh,” SAFF announced during the draw ceremony for the SAFF Championship in Thimpu, Bhutan, on Saturday.

Bangladesh were drawn into Group A alongside Sri Lanka and Bhutan, while Group B comprises India, Pakistan and the Maldives.

But Nepal needs the FIFA suspension, which was imposed on June 24 citing continuous third-party interference, to be lifted. And it is only possible when the incumbent ANFA President Pankaj Bikram Nembang’s plan for an early election is allowed to resume from the point it was stopped in Jhapa on March 26 after the government’s intervention.

Nembang is allowed to host an early election, and it abides by FIFA and ANFA Statutes, the governing body of international football has stated multiple times. However, the National Sports Council (NSC) has had a separate opinion that ANFA can conduct its elections only after ensuring a fresh mandate at the district associations.

“It is not a fair election if there are the same voters, who helped Nembang win the previous election, at the district level,” the NSC has been stressing.

Despite Nembang’s four-year term ending only in mid-June, he had put forth the plan to organise it as early as February. “We cannot force district associations to conduct their elections before time because they are independent bodies,” Kiran Rai, ANFA general secretary, has been defending Nembang’s move.

With the two authorities—ANFA and NSC—at loggerheads, the NSC even had ANFA suspended for up to three months on March 25, two days before ANFA’s election in Jhapa. It was later lifted following warnings of suspension from FIFA, but ANFA was still under state scrutiny.

It was only after the government disallowed ANFA representatives from flying abroad to participate in FIFA’s Congress, Summit and World Cup that the international footballing body had enough and imposed the suspension.

FIFA’s suspension means that Nepali football cannot exercise any of its membership rights. “Other member associations may not entertain sporting contact with a suspended member association,” FIFA stated in a circular to all of its members.

As a result, Nepal could not participate in the AFC Women’s Champions League 2026/27, AFC U17 Women’s Asian Cup Qualifiers and AFC U20 Asian Cup Qualifiers.

Had Nepal’s suspension been lifted by August 1, Nepal, who were drawn in Group I alongside Mongolia, Guam and Northern Mariana Islands on May 28, could have had the opportunity to play in the U20 Qualifiers. Now, the fixtures are out, and Nepal are not listed in the group.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC), on June 27, had written a letter to ANFA stating that the deadlines to lift the FIFA suspension in order to ensure participation at the Women’s Champions League and U17 Women’s Asian Cup Qualifiers were on June 29 and July 13, respectively. As the suspension continued, Nepal were excluded.

However, Nepal had lost two other footballing events, long before the FIFA suspension, to the tussle between ANFA and NSC.

Firstly, a friendly between the men’s teams of Nepal and Hong Kong scheduled for March 26 was cancelled after the NSC, as per ANFA, did not allow the use of Dasharath Stadium. The NSC, meanwhile, defended itself by making public permission letters provided to ANFA.

Secondly, Nepal women’s team could not travel to Thailand in mid-April for the FIFA Series as ANFA withdrew from the tournament citing NSC’s suspension. The women’s team were training in a closed camp for the Series when they heard the bad news.

As they were denied participation in the FIFA Series, the women’s team could not train properly during the closed camp for the SAFF Women’s Championship, which Nepal played in Goa, India, from May 25.

“There were noises of FIFA suspension when the team was training. As they had missed the FIFA Series already, they were in continuous fear of missing the SAFF tournament as well,” Nabin Neupane, the team’s head coach, had told the Post earlier. “They were not focused on training. How could they even?”

Neupane also took to social media on Sunday and requested the government to take necessary steps to ensure the men’s team did not lose the opportunity.

“Honourable Prime Minister, the SAFF Championship is like the World Cup to us. It is not merely a tournament—it is an opportunity tied to the dreams, hard work, and futures of thousands of Nepali players and coaches,” Neupane, who is also a former national player, wrote. “Considering the future of Nepali footballers, please create a suitable environment to play.”

Similarly, Nepal’s captain Kiran Chemjong posted a photo of the teams divided into two groups for the SAFF Championship on his Facebook story. He then wrote, “As a proud Nepali footballer, seeing Nepal’s name missing from the upcoming SAFF schedule is heartbreaking.”

He added, “We have always fought for our country with pride, passion and hope,” Chemjong continued. “We sincerely hope that the ban will be lifted soon and that Nepal will once again be on the pitch, representing our nation and making our people proud.”

Manish Dangi, another national player, had also requested the same from the state.

The Post has been trying to reach out to Minister for Education and Sports Sasmit Pokharel and the ministry’s spokesperson Shiva Kumar Sapkota for comments for weeks. However, they have not responded despite repetitive calls and messages.

Minister Pokharel had publicly stated a couple of weeks ago that the government was in communication with FIFA and AFC and had called their representatives for dialogue. He has not spoken about the issue since then.

The Post has also sought a response from FIFA on the matter through the formal channel for media.

title: Opinion | Nepal’s problematic foreign policy: Symbols without substance - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Nepal’s problematic foreign policy: Symbols without substance  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The greatest problem among Nepali politicians is that they lose the opportunity at hand and indulge in blame games to hide their failures. This has happened since the dawn of democracy in 1951 and continues to this day. Most of the time, opportunities were squandered due to a lack of direction and attempts to falsify politics by pointing fingers at a foreign hand, making foreign policy a mobilising strategy to score domestic political gains, particularly at a time when the regime faced a survival crisis. In the post-1960 decades, the consolidation of power for individual aggrandisement and ambition sidetracked the development agenda.

Mixing unclarified concepts with the actual practice of foreign policy has not only obfuscated the issues but also misdirected the executioners. Many such concepts might have symbolic value, but symbols without substance hardly make any progress. Concepts such as the policy of equidistance might be theoretically correct, but they carry no meaning when applied to Nepal’s relations with China and India.

The veritable Nepal-India relations cannot be equated with China, as mainland China is still a distant neighbour despite making Tibet its integral part. Facing south of the Himalayas, and sharing geographical, economic, cultural and humanitarian commonalities, Nepal continues to rely on India in many respects. Thus, even while asserting Nepal’s nationalism and independence, the Nepali power elites have not attempted to dilute the structural relations defined by history as well as by the doctrine of necessity. For China, Nepal must maintain cordial relations without harming China’s vital security interest pertaining to Tibet. Other dimensions are changing as circumstances demand, as has happened with trade and transit.

Concepts such as upgrading Nepal’s landlocked status to land-linked status, as the Chinese President suggested during his visit to Nepal in 2019, and later promoted by other Nepali analysts, seem far-fetched, if not absurd. In the modern world, such a proposition can be implemented only with the priority to be given by China. And China is not likely to invest a huge amount to develop rail links without eyeing the Indian market, as the Nepali market is too small to fulfil Chinese economic objectives. If China and India fail to enter into some sort of an entente cordiale, and continue their longstanding border conflict along with undeclared competition for guaranteeing security to each other, Nepal can neither be a bridge between China and India nor would the Chinese be inclined to raise the level of development across the Himalayas.

It is assumed that China is not interested in resolving the border problem with India, as it believes it may continue to engage India in what the former foreign secretary of India, Vijay Gokhle, terms ‘grey zone coercion’ that neither ends the hostility nor goes in for a war. Indians also know that since China does not take India as its peer competitor in international politics, China would like to see India not be too close to the US, its principal competitor for hegemony in world politics. Nepal’s importance lies in its location straddling between China (Tibet) and India, and not for other reasons.

Another concept, dui dhunga bich ko tarul (yam between two stones), might have had its validity in the past, but it is no longer so. Nepal’s exposure to the outside world since the end of the Rana oligarchy has changed the dynamics on both the internal and external fronts. Internally, Nepal has passed through several political upheavals, including the transformation from monarchy to republic. Externally, it has established links with other distant countries across the globe, gaining a new status as a fully sovereign, independent country. Nevertheless, its geopolitical constraints cannot be overlooked when asserting national aspirations.

It has been argued today that the US is as influential as other immediate neighbours in steering Nepal’s course of development. As a superpower, the US still exercises its leverage, making China and India uncomfortable with its increased role in their vicinity. Even otherwise, Nepal’s scope of foreign policy has expanded to the extent of playing an important role in maintaining peace under the auspices of the UN.

The other buzzword is ‘strategic autonomy’ that carries little sense in the context of world politics. This concept is used to balance the two neighbours, particularly by taking advantage of their adversarial relationship. While consolidating the royal regime in the 1960s, King Mahendra used it between 1961-70, but later recanted his strategy, knowing that his manoeuvrability was over when India emerged as a regional power after playing a ‘midwifery role’ in creating the new republic of Bangladesh. King Birendra’s policy failed when India didn’t endorse his peace zone proposal despite the overwhelming support of other countries, including China. Nepal’s decision to issue a new map incorporating Limpiadhura, Lipulekh and Kalapani seems to have been stuck following India’s refusal to accept them as Nepali territory. Instead of using the chuche naksha as evidence for negotiations, Nepali political leaders rushed it to the Parliament to make it a constitutional organ.

Nepal’s foreign policy initiatives have shrunk in recent years. The main reasons are uncalled-for mobilising rhetoric, miscalculation and a lack of objectivity in weighing the pros and cons of any decision taken at the whim of the leaders. Their failure to resist any pressure in making wrong decisions also produced unproductive results. The present Balendra Shah-led government is increasingly problematic in domestic politics and foreign policy. Since the prime minister’s strange behaviour and style of governance do not match the letter and spirit of the multiparty parliamentary system, no one knows which system of government he is heading. There has been a trust deficit in Nepal’s China and India policies, notwithstanding the foreign minister’s visits to New Delhi and Beijing to restore the neighbours’ confidence.

title: Editorial | Why Nepal’s secular fabric is facing its toughest test yet - The Kathmandu Post
description: Editorial | Why Nepal’s secular fabric is facing its toughest test yet  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The recent unrest in Tarai-Madhesh, triggered by a communal clash in Devanganj, Sunsari, on July 26, has reminded Nepal of its vulnerability to religious friction. The Nepali state has historically relied upon coercive force to maintain fragile peace. Such reactive measures are insufficient to address the undercurrents currently threatening the nation’s social fabric. It is now a matter of national urgency that the government initiates a rigorous and transparent investigation into the burgeoning influence and tactical operations of extremist religious outfits whose activities are increasingly linked to the propagation of religious hate in Nepal.

Nepal’s modern political identity was built upon a foundation of secular mobilisation, which has long existed in a state of tension with a historically Hinduised state structure. This friction has been exacerbated over the last decade, as political actors began instrumentalising religion for mobilisation. The rise of a religion-centric power structure in neighbouring states has further catalysed the shift in Nepal, empowering the religious organisations to mobilise resources across the border and expand their networks.

The methodology of this expansion warrants intense scrutiny. Alarmingly, current trends indicate the adoption of fluid organisational structures as a deliberate strategy to evade accountability. Rather than operating through identifiable entities, various groups are rapidly formed under innocuous banners only to be dissolved or rebranded once their immediate objectives of spreading religious rhetoric are achieved. This tactic, likely imported from contemporary practices in neighbouring states, makes it nearly impossible for journalists, researchers, or auditors to track funding sources and institutional affiliations. The state, therefore, seems to be the only mechanism capable of tracing the external influence on such organisations.

The reported involvement of retired high-ranking security officials, including former generals, with these religious-political organisations is another concern for national security. The recruitment of such individuals provides radical networks with tactical knowledge required to manipulate community-level violence. Meanwhile, the security apparatus remains characterised by an institutionalised insensitivity and a command mentality that prioritises punishment over dialogue. When the state relies on the indiscriminate use of force, coupled with former high-level security officials joining radical networks, it enables radical networks to use violence to rattle the social fabric.

The current administration’s failure to address the underlying causes of communal triggers is no longer tenable. The state’s historical amnesia regarding the roots of communal violence allows radical groups like the Hindu Samrat Sena to benefit from a fragmented landscape while maintaining links to extremist ideologies.

A meaningful response to this crisis requires more than traditional nationalist rhetoric, temporary curfews, or solidarity rallies. The authorities must empower the civil society of regional hubs, such as Biratnagar and Janakpur, to conduct autonomous investigations into communal incidents rather than waiting for orders from a centralised and often distracted leadership in Kathmandu. There must also be a concerted effort to foster an informed and critical citizenship capable of engaging in dialogue before tensions spiral into violence. Concurrently, the security forces need to be trained extensively in conflict de-escalation.

The preservation of Nepal’s secular identity demands that the state confront the opaque funding and fluid tactics of the organisations linked to extremist religious outfits. Failure to investigate these networks will only signal to the public—and to the international community—that the rule of law has been surrendered to the interests of imported religious radicalism.

title: How Nepal’s gym culture is growing beyond the young generation - The Kathmandu Post
description: How Nepal’s gym culture is growing beyond the young generation  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
“Social media definitely plays its part. Viewers see reels online of others working out. There are many fitness creators in Nepal pushing people to work out and explaining the benefits of doing so. That challenges traditional beliefs. It is not only Nepali creators. People have access to content from all over the world. Fitness content has always been big in the West, and as Nepali viewers see more of that, it changes who comes to workout,” Shrestha says.

Moktan adds, "Schools used to focus on education. That was the only thing that mattered – you had to study well. Now, most schools also focus on extracurricular activities and fitness as important things. If children come home with a certain idea, or if parents see what schools are focusing on, that helps to change people’s perceptions too.”

“Doctors are also to thank for the increase in older people going to the gym. Doctors will recommend their patients go to the gym to help them counteract loss of strength or if they have high cholesterol and other such things,” Moktan said.

“The gym is a preventive thing. It helps reduce the risk of health complications. Doctors will send patients to the gym if something goes wrong, but medical professionals should be telling people to start working out so things don’t get a chance to go wrong,” he also added.

There are still ways in which working out at the gym is seen in a negative light.

“Parents will tell their kids that so-and-so's kid went to the gym and got injured in such-and-such way, so you shouldn’t go. Another popular misconception is that working out at a young age will stop you from getting taller. There are many other misconceptions. It is not that everybody, suddenly, has adopted good sources of information. People have, but most have not,” Shrestha said.

People’s source of information repeatedly came up as the primary reason for the change in demographics but also the main problem in the industry.

“The gym has a lot of things that are new to a lot of people. For example, with diets, we recommend people eat a certain way so they can gain muscle. It is very common that our clients do not get enough protein. Clients do listen to us, but the people coming here are already better informed than most. It shows how well informed the average person might be,” Shrestha said.

मोक्तान आगू कहैत छथि, "पहिने स्कूल शिक्षा पर ध्यान दैत छल. एतबे टा बात छल जे महत्व रखैत छल – नीक पढ़ाई करय पड़ैत छल. आब, अधिकांश स्कूल सेहो पाठ्येतर गतिविधि आ फिटनेस पर सेहो महत्वपूर्ण बातक रूप मे ध्यान दैत अछि. जँ बच्चा सभ कोनो खास विचार ल’ क’ घर अबैत अछि, वा जँ अभिभावक देखैत छथि जे स्कूल कोन बात पर ध्यान केंद्रित क’ रहल अछि, त’ ओहि सँ लोकक धारणा सेहो बदलबा मे मददि भेटैत अछि.”

मोक्तान कहलनि जे, डॉक्टर के जिम जाय वाला उम्र बढ़ला के लेल सेहो धन्यवाद देबय के अछि, डॉक्टर अपन मरीज के जिम जेबाक सलाह देत, जाहि सं हुनकर ताकत के नुकसान के रोकय में मदद मिलत या अगर हुनका में कोलेस्ट्रॉल आ एहन अन्य चीज बेसी अछि त हुनकर मदद मिलत।

ओ इहो कहलनि जे, जिम एकटा निवारक चीज अछि, स्वास्थ्य संबंधी जटिलता के खतरा कम करय मे मदद करैत अछि, डॉक्टर मरीज के जिम भेजताह अगर किछ गड़बड़ी भ जायत, मुदा मेडिकल प्रोफेशनल के लोक के कहय के चाही जे वर्कआउट शुरू करू ताकि चीज गलत होबय के मौका नहि मिलय.

एखनो एहन तरीका अछि जे जिम मे वर्कआउट कए नकारात्मक नजरि मे देखल जाइत अछि।

"माता-पिता अपन बच्चा सभकेँ कहताह जे फल्लाँक बच्चा जिम गेल आ फल्लाँ तरहेँ घायल भ' गेल, तेँ अहाँकेँ नहि जेबाक चाही. एकटा आओर लोकप्रिय गलतफहमी ई अछि जे कम उम्र मे वर्कआउट कर' सँ अहाँ लंबा होब' सँ रोकि देत. आओर बहुत रास गलतफहमी अछि. एहन नहि जे सभ कियो, अचानक, नीक जानकारीक स्रोत अपना लेने अछि. लोक सभ केने अछि, मुदा बेसी लोक नहि केने अछि." श्रेष्ठ बजलीह।

जनसांख्यिकीय परिवर्तन केरऽ प्राथमिक कारण के रूप म॑ बार-बार लोगऽ के जानकारी के स्रोत सामने ऐलै लेकिन उद्योग म॑ मुख्य समस्या भी ।

श्रेष्ठ कहला जे जिम मे बहुत रास चीज अछि जे बहुत लोक लेल नव अछि।उदाहरण लेल आहार क संग हम लोक कए एकटा खास तरीका स भोजन करबाक सलाह दैत छी ताकि हुनका मांसपेशी बढ़ि सकए, इ बहुत आम बात अछि जे हमर ग्राहक कए पर्याप्त प्रोटीन नहि भेटैत अछि। ग्राहक हमरा सबहक गप जरूर सुनैत छथि, मुदा एतय आबय वाला लोक कए बेसी स बेसी जानकारी पहिने स नीक अछि। एहि स इ पता चलैत अछि जे औसत व्यक्ति कतेक नीक जानकारी भ सकैत अछि।

मोक्तान मुस्कुराइत अपन बात समाप्त करैत कहैत छथि, "हमर सभक काजक हिस्सा सेहो अछि जे लोक केँ नीक जकाँ जानकारी भेटय आ ई बुझल जाय जे ओ की क’ रहल छथि आ किएक। मुदा हम सभ असगर सभक सोच केँ नहि बदलि सकैत छी। समाजक आन सदस्य जिनकर आवाज महत्वपूर्ण अछि, हुनका सेहो बजबाक आवश्यकता अछि।"

title: Nepal Seeks India’s Nod for Its National Identity Card in Cross-Border Travel - The Financial World
description: Nepal Seeks India’s Nod for Its National Identity Card in Cross-Border Travel  The Financial World
publisher.title: The Financial World
full_article:
Kathmandu: Nepal has formally requested India to recognise its National Identity Card (NID) as a valid travel document for cross-border travel, aiming to strengthen identity verification and security while facilitating the movement of people between the two countries, a senior immigration official said.

The NID is similar to India’s Aadhaar card and contains biometric information, including fingerprints, facial images and iris scans. The Nepali government has made the NID mandatory for accessing several public services, including passport applications, land registration, opening bank accounts and other government services, as it seeks to gradually replace the traditional citizenship certificate with digitally readable identity cards.

Nepal also wants India to recognise the NID as a valid document for the cross-border movement of Nepali citizens, as India currently recognises Nepal’s passport and citizenship certificate as official identity documents. Citizens of Nepal and India are not required to carry passports or visas to travel between the two countries.

Ram Chandra Tiwari, director general of the Department of Immigration, told IANS that his office sent a proposal to the Government of India in late June seeking recognition of the NID as a valid travel document for Nepali citizens.

“At present, India recognises mainly Nepal’s passport and citizenship certificate as official identity documents. We have formally proposed that the National Identity Card also be accepted as a valid identification document for air travel and cross-border movement,” Tiwari said.

Following Nepal’s request, officials from the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu recently sought information from Nepal’s immigration authorities about the NID.

“The embassy officials made informal inquiries regarding the card’s technical and security aspects. It was not a formal bilateral meeting but an exchange of information,” Tiwari said.

He said the NID offers stronger security than the traditional citizenship certificate.

“A citizenship certificate is merely a paper document without biometric information, whereas the NID provides a secure and reliable means of identification. Its recognition would enhance security arrangements for both Nepal and India,” he added.

More than 4.5 million Nepali citizens have already received the National Identity Card, while around 20 million people have enrolled for one, according to the Department of National ID and Civil Registration.

title: Managing Urban Floods - The Rising Nepal
description: Managing Urban Floods  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Every monsoon, the same sorry show of waterlogged roads, houses submerged, vehicles stalled, drains overflowing and families waiting to be rescued is repeated in Nepal’s cities. The catastrophic flood that engulfed Kathmandu in late September 2024 revealed that urban flooding is no longer an occasional inconvenience. It’s a major crisis for infrastructure and public safety. Heavy rain was the trigger, but unplanned construction, shrinking river corridors, paved open land, clogged drains and weak coordination turned heavy rain into disaster.

Once upon a time, the Kathmandu Valley was a place of rivers, ponds, wetlands, agricultural fields and traditional stone spouts that stored, absorbed and slowly released water. Much of this natural system has been lost to buildings, roads and concrete surfaces as a result of rapid urbanisation. Rainwater that used to soak into the ground now rushes into undersized drains and swollen rivers. Things are no different in Lalitpur, Biratnagar, Pokhara, Butwal and other fast-growing cities.

And the answer is not simply to build bigger drains along the road. Nepal needs an integrated urban water-management system, with engineering, land-use planning and ecological restoration.

First, every municipality should develop a digital stormwater master plan. Engineers can use rainfall records, topographic surveys, satellite images and hydraulic models to identify streets prone to flooding, blocked channels, and locations where new drains, culverts, pumping stations or temporary storage are needed. Drainage infrastructure should be designed for the future intensity of rainfall, not out-of-date historical averages. Wherever possible, stormwater drains should be separated from sewer lines. In heavy rain, mixed systems overflow, dumping polluted water into homes and streets.

Second, Kathmandu needs to protect the Bagmati, Bishnumati, Manohara, Nakhu and other river corridors. Floodplains should be mapped, legally defined and kept free of further construction. Public greenways and overflow space should be restored with vegetation on riverbanks. Engineering structures can protect critical locations, but confining rivers between concrete walls can transfer flood risk downstream.

Third, cities should implement “sponge city” measures. Rain gardens, permeable pavements, detention ponds, recharge pits, rooftop harvesting and restored wetlands can all capture rain close to its point of fall. Schools, government buildings, residential colonies, shopping malls and industrial areas should be made to hold back a part of their stormwater before it is let out into the city drains. These decentralised systems are often cheaper and more flexible than relying only on huge underground pipes.

Fourth, maintenance must be a year-round municipal service. Plastic, sediment and construction waste clog even the best-designed drains and cause failure. There must be mandatory pre-monsoon inspection, mechanical cleaning, waste control and public reporting of choked drains. Utility agencies need to coordinate road digging so as not to damage or bury water channels.

Finally, engineering has to be complemented by real-time rainfall monitoring, river sensors, neighbourhood sirens, mobile alerts and clearly marked evacuation routes. Flood maps should inform decisions about building permits, emergency shelters and insurance. Local communities need to know not only that danger is coming, but where to go, and which roads are still safe. Funding should be a combination of federal grants, municipal revenues and developer contributions, with the most vulnerable settlements taking precedence.

Urban flooding can't be totally wiped out, particularly when climate change means more extreme rain. But the number of deaths, damage and disruption can be greatly lessened. Nepal’s cities need to stop treating each monsoon flood as an isolated natural disaster. It’s an engineering and governance issue, and it’s predictable. It will cost far less to prevent than to rebuild, compensate, and lose livelihoods repeatedly.

title: Time to promote Nepali brands: Minister Yadav - The Rising Nepal
description: Time to promote Nepali brands: Minister Yadav  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Aug 4: Minister for Industry, Commerce and Supplies, Gauri Kumari Yadav, has urged industrialists and businesspersons to receive Nepal Standard (NS) Mark for their products in order to promote domestic products, ensure quality and reduce dependence on imports.

The use of NS Mark is imperative for the development of quality domestic products and market expansion, she underlined during a discussion with officials of the Department of Standards and Metrology. It is time to expand the scope of NS Mark, according to her.

NS Mark not only facilitates in selling and distributing products produced in Nepal to the international market but also boosts consumers' confidence. The government has decided to provide necessary incentives to businesspersons and ease the process of obtaining NS Mark, the Minister shared.

Various industrial products including cement, rods and tires produced in Nepal have received the NS Mark.

Lately, sanitary pads produced in Nepal have got the NS Mark. The Ministry has urged the industries and companies to complete necessary processes on time to get the essential mark, ensuring quality products. (RSS)
